headline: High risk of capability conflict and cascading errors; prompt-injection and leakage are lower but non-zero due to shared filesystem and broad shell/network access.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read and write files, and A’s plan-local sandbox plus B’s local development environment create a plausible file-based bridge. B also exposes multiple API surfaces and may treat file content as trusted. No direct shared channel is documented, so this is inferred and uncertain.
conditions: IF A writes attacker-controlled instructions into a shared project file that B later reads
IF B ingests file contents as trusted prompts or task context without provenance checks
mitigations: Separate working directories for A and B
Disable auto-ingest of repository files into B prompts
Add a provenance banner to all inter-agent files
Review any shared markdown or config before B consumes it

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches source code and has broad network egress; B touches academic papers, metadata, research questions, and configuration secrets. If they share a workspace or files, either can expose the other’s sensitive context through outputs or network calls. The exact sharing mechanism is not documented, so uncertainty pushes this to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF A and B operate on the same filesystem or synced workspace
IF B sends paper metadata or secrets to external APIs during normal operation
mitigations: Use separate workspaces and credentials
Redact secrets before any shared handoff
Block network egress for files containing secrets
Audit B’s API calls for sensitive payloads
requires-engineering: add automatic secret scanning before handoff

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A can modify git state and write the filesystem; B can also write the filesystem and run shell commands. A’s concurrency model explicitly mentions shared state via a Plandex backend, while B supports multiple instances but does not state locking. That makes concurrent writes to shared mutable resources a realistic default hazard.
conditions: IF both agents target the same git repository or directory
IF B performs file edits while A stages or applies changes
mitigations: Assign disjoint directories per agent
Serialize write access with a simple operator checklist
Pause one agent before the other applies changes
Avoid concurrent git operations
requires-engineering: add file-locking or transaction coordination

D_cascading_error.rationale: A is a planner with review-then-apply behavior, and B is a content-writing/RAG agent with ask/agentic-ask endpoints. If B consumes A’s generated plans or facts without verification, errors can propagate into downstream outputs. No direct action-taking authority is documented, so medium fits better than high.
conditions: IF B uses A’s plan text or code suggestions as authoritative input
IF downstream outputs are generated without an explicit verification step
mitigations: Require a human review step between agents
Force B to cite source files before acting
Compare A’s output against repository state
Limit B to drafting only, not execution
requires-engineering: add automated validation of A-to-B handoffs

E_compliance.rationale: B explicitly handles configuration secrets and academic/paper data, while A handles model-provider API keys and source code. If either agent processes regulated or sensitive data under different retention or residency assumptions, a compliance mismatch is plausible. The profiles do not document a specific jurisdiction mismatch, so this remains medium.
conditions: IF either agent processes personal data, secrets, or regulated research data under different retention rules
IF one agent’s logs or exports are retained longer than the other’s
mitigations: Align retention settings before use
Keep secrets out of shared prompts
Document data-class handling for both agents
Review export and deletion behavior
requires-engineering: implement policy-based retention controls
